Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 25, verses 1–3:

(p-416) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir of Surat al-Furqan (the Criterion)

This surah is Meccan according to the majority (al-jumhur). al-Dahhak said: it is Madani, and within it are Meccan verses, namely His saying: ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another god﴾ [al-Furqan: 68] and the verses that follow.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Blessed is He who sent down the Criterion upon His servant that he may be a warner to the worlds﴾ ﴿He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He has not taken a son, and there is not for Him a partner in dominion, and He created everything and determined it with [precise] determination.﴾ ﴿Yet they have taken, besides Him, deities that create nothing, while they are created, and they possess not for themselves any harm or benefit, and they possess not death or life or resurrection.﴾

"Tabaraka" is of the measure tafā'ala, and it is a verb in the present tense. "Baraka" derives from barakah (blessing), and "bāraka" is a verb of the form fā'ala from one party, meaning "increased." "Tabaraka" is a verb specific to Allah the Exalted; it is not used for anyone else, and for this reason no future tense or active participle is derived from it. It is a descriptive verb, meaning: His blessings have multiplied, and among them is the sending down of His Book, which is the Criterion (al-furqan) between truth and falsehood. The opening of this verse is in fact a response to statements that were made by the Quraysh. Among them was their saying: "The Qur'an is merely something Muhammad has fabricated, and it is not from Allah," and this verse is a response to these statements.

al-Jumhur read: "upon His servant (ʿabdihi)," while ʿAbdullah ibn al-Zubayr read: "upon His servants (ʿibādihi)." The pronoun in His saying "that he may be (li-yakūna)" may refer to Muhammad ﷺ, who is the servant mentioned, and this is the interpretation of Ibn Zayd; or it may refer to the Qur'an. As for the reading of Ibn al-Zubayr, it refers to the Qur'an and cannot bear any other meaning except with difficulty. His saying, Exalted is He: "to the worlds (lil-ʿalamīn)" is general, covering every human and jinn, whether they were contemporaries of his or came after him, and this is confirmed by numerous ahadith that are mutawatir and by the apparent meaning of the verses. "Nadhir" (warner) is one who warns against evil. A messenger from Allah is a nadhir, and a nadhir may be one who is not a messenger, as has been related concerning Dhu'l-Qarnayn, and as occurs concerning the messengers of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to the jinn, for they are nudhur (warners) and not rusul (messengers).

His saying, Exalted is He: "He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth," the verse is part of the response to the Quraysh in their saying "Allah has a partner," and in their saying "He has taken daughters," and in their saying in the talbiyah: "There is no partner, except a partner who belongs to You." His saying, Exalted is He: "and He created everything" is general, covering every created thing. The determination (taqdir) of things is their limitation by places, times, quantities, benefit, and perfect craftsmanship.

Then, Exalted is He, after mentioning these attributes which belong to divinity, He follows with a reproach to the Quraysh for taking as gods those who do not possess these attributes; reason thus indicates that they are not gods. His saying, Exalted is He: "while they are created (wa-hum yukhlaqun)" may mean: Allah creates them by origination and bringing into existence; and it may mean: they are created by humans through carving and carpentry. This latter interpretation more clearly reveals the lowliness of the idols. The creation of humans is permissible, but the Arabs use the word for it, and from it is the saying of Zuhayr:

"And indeed you smooth out what you have created, while some people create and then do not smooth out."

This is derived from khalaqtu al-jild (I created the hide), when I make markings on it that are then cut along; so al-fary is to cut along the traced markings. His saying, Exalted is He: "death or life (mawtan wa-la hayatan)" means: causing death or causing life. "Nushur" means the raising of people from their graves.

(p-٤١٨) His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿Those who disbelieve say: "This is nothing but a fabrication which he has invented, and other people have helped him with it." Indeed, they have come with injustice and falsehood.﴾ ﴿And they say: "Tales of the ancients, which he has had written down, and they are dictated to him morning and evening."﴾ ﴿Say: "It was sent down by the One who knows the secret in the heavens and the earth. Indeed, He is ever Forgiving, Merciful."﴾

What is meant by ﴿those who disbelieve﴾ is Quraysh. Some of them said: "This is a lie which Muhammad has invented." People differed about those who were said to be helping Muhammad ﷺ, according to the claim of Quraysh. Mujahid said: they pointed to a group of Jews. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: they pointed to slaves of the Arabs who were Persians, one of whom was Abu Fakiha, a freedman of the Hadramis, and Jabr, Yasar, 'Addas, and others. Then God, may He be exalted, informed about them that they had not come except with wrongdoing and falsehood, meaning that they said nothing but slander and falsehood. And *al-zur* (falsehood, forgery) in common usage means making falsehood appear attractive, but its original sense is embellishment in general. From this is the saying of 'Umar, may God be pleased with him: "So I wanted to put before Abu Bakr a statement that I had embellished (*zawwartuha*)."

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and they say: "Tales of the ancients"﴾, Ibn 'Abbas said: by this is meant the saying of al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. They said: everything in the Qur'an that mentions "tales of the ancients" is only because of al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who was well known for this. Then they accused Muhammad ﷺ that he had had them written down. Talha ibn Musarrif read *uktutibaha* (with the first *ta'* vowelled with a *damma* and the second with a *kasra*), meaning: they were written down for him. Abu al-Fath (Ibn Jinni) mentioned this. Talha also read *tutla* with a *ta'* in place of the *mim*. Then God, may He be exalted, commanded him to say: the One who sent it down is God, who knows the secret of all things that are in the heavens and the earth. Then He informed that He is Forgiving and Merciful, so that every listener may hope for His pardon and mercy together with repentance and turning back to Him. The meaning is that God is Forgiving and Merciful in leaving those who hold these sayings and disbelief (to continue), so that perhaps they will believe.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 25, verses 7–10:

(p-419) His Exalted and Majestic saying:

﴿And they said, "What is with this Messenger? He eats food and walks in the markets. Why has an angel not been sent down to him so that he might be a warner with him?"﴾ ﴿Or a treasure be thrown down to him, or he have a garden from which he may eat?" And the wrongdoers said, "You are only following a man affected by magic."﴾ ﴿Look how they coin comparisons for you, so they have gone astray and cannot find a way.﴾ ﴿Blessed is He who, if He wills, shall give you better than that: gardens beneath which rivers flow, and He shall give you palaces.﴾

The pronoun in His saying "they said" refers to the Quraysh. This is because they had a well-known gathering with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), which Ibn Ishaq mentioned in the *Sirah* and others. Its content is that their leaders, 'Utba and others, gathered with him and said: "O Muhammad, if you desire leadership, we will make you our ruler; and if you desire wealth, we will gather wealth for you from our possessions." When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) refused, they returned to the matter of disputing with him and said to him: "What is the matter with you? Although you are a messenger from Allah, you eat food and stand in the markets seeking provision?" That is, one who was the Messenger of Allah should be independent of all of that. Then they said to him: "Ask your Lord to send down with you an angel to warn along with you, or to throw down to you a treasure from which you may spend, or to return the mountains of Makkah to you as gold, or to remove the mountains and have in their place gardens through which water flows." They spread this argument, and this verse was revealed.

The letter *lam* in "*mal hadha*" was written separately from the words of their saying. This is either because the Mushaf follows the cut-off pronunciation of the word, so the scribe followed it; or because they saw that the prepositions were detached from what follows them, like *min*, *fi*, *'an* and *'ala*. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read *yakulu minha* with the *ya'* (yā'). Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *nakulu* with the *nun* (nūn), and this is the reading of Ibn Wathhab, Ibn Musarrif and Sulayman ibn Mihran.

Then Allah, exalted is He, informed about them, namely the wrongdoers to whom reference has been made, that they (p-420) said, when they had despaired of Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿You are only following a man affected by magic.﴾ It is possible that "*masḥūr*" is derived from *sihr*, which means the windpipe (*ri'a*), so that they meant to belittle him, that is, a man like you in physical form. This was mentioned by Makki and others. Then Allah, exalted is He, alerted him, consoling him regarding their statement, and said: ﴿Look how they coin comparisons for you, so they have gone astray﴾, that is, they missed the path, so they do not find a way to guidance, and they are not able to reach it, because they are embroiled in its opposite, which is error.

His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Blessed is He who﴾ and the rest of the verse is a return of Muhammad's (ﷺ) affairs to Allah. That is: this is your direction, not the direction of these erring people regarding your affair. The reference of "*dhalika*" (that): Mujahid said it refers to what the disbelievers mentioned of a treasure and a garden in this world. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said it refers to his eating food and walking in the markets. al-Tabari said: the first is more apparent.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Because the second interpretation gives the impression that the gardens and palaces mentioned in this verse are in this world, and this is the interpretation of al-Tha'labi and others. His saying after that refutes it: ﴿Nay, they denied the Hour﴾ [al-Furqan: 11]. All of them are possible.

'Asim, according to the narration of Abu Bakr and Hafs, and Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *wa-yaj'al* with a *jazm* (jazm), upon the position of the response in His saying *ja'ala*, because the intended meaning is: if He wills, He will make. Abu Bakr also reported from 'Asim, as did Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir, *wa-yaj'alu* with a *raf'* (ḍamma) and *isti'nāf* (resumption), and this is the reading of Mujahid. Its basis is the coordination upon the meaning in His saying *ja'ala*, because the response of the conditional is the position of a new sentence. Do you not see that a clause consisting of a subject and predicate may occupy the position of the response of the conditional? 'Abd Allah ibn Musa and Talha ibn Sulayman read *wa-yaj'ala* with a *naṣb* (fatḥa) (p-421), and it is upon the assumption of *an* at the beginning of the speech. Abu al-Fath said: it is upon the response of the condition. They said: this is a weak reading. al-A'raj assimilated *ja'l laka* and *yaj'al laka*, and this was transmitted from Ibn Muhaysin.

"*Al-qusur*" (palaces) are houses built with walls, as said by Mujahid and others. The Arabs used to call what was made of hair, wool and reeds a *bayt* (house), and they called what was built with walls a *qasr* (palace), because it *qassara* (was shortened) from those who entered it.

"Wa-a'tadna" means: We made ready, and al-'ataad (provision) is what is prepared of things. And "al-sa'ir" is a layer of the layers of Jahannam (Hell).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When it sees them﴾ means: Jahannam, since the word "sa'ir" necessitates it. The word "ra'at-hum" may be taken literally, or may be taken figuratively in the sense: it becomes, from them, to the extent that the beholder sees from a distance. However, there is a hadith which requires the literal sense in this matter, mentioned by al-Tabari, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever lies about me deliberately, let him take his seat in the Fire between the two eyes of Jahannam." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, does Jahannam have two eyes?" He said: "Recite, if you wish: ﴿When it sees them from a distant place﴾." It is also narrated in some reports that the distance from which it sees them is the journey of a year, and it is narrated that it is the journey of five hundred years.

(p-422) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿they will hear its raging and roaring﴾ is a word containing metaphor (tajawwuz), because raging (taghayyuz) is not heard; rather, what is heard are sounds indicating the raging, and these are, without doubt, blazings within the Fire like what is heard in the fire of this world. So the relation of what is heard in this world to that is the relation of burning to burning, and it is seventy times, as occurs in the Sahih. And "al-zafir" is a prolonged sound like the sound of a donkey drawing out its braying. Al-Naqqash said: "al-Zafir is the sound of a donkey at its braying." 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: "Indeed Jahannam will emit a single exhalation such that no angel or prophet remains but falls prostrate, his limbs trembling."

And "the narrow place" within it is an intent to constrict them in place within the Fire, and that is a kind of punishment. The Prayer and peace be upon him said: "Indeed they will be made to enter the Fire as a peg is driven into a wall," that is: they enter unwillingly and forcibly. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "It constricts them as the butt-spike constricts the spear on the spear-shaft." Ibn Kathir, and 'Ubayd from Abu 'Amr, read "dayyiqan" with the yaa lightened; the rest read it with the yaa doubled.

The meaning of "muqarranin" is: bound one to another. It is narrated that this is with chains of fire. And "al-qarinan" among oxen are two that are yoked together with a rope for ploughing, and from this is the poet's saying:

"When the rope of the two yoked ones continues to twist, a day will surely come when the strands are severed."

Abu Shayba al-Muhri, companion of Mu'adh ibn Jabal (may Allah be pleased with him), read "muqarrinun" with a waw, and this is an irregular reading (shadhdha), while the correct one is the people's reading. His saying "thuburan" is a verbal noun (masdar), and is not the one called upon; the object of "da'aw" is omitted, its estimated form being: they call upon one who does not answer them, and similar to this of estimations.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is also valid that "al-thubur" be the one called upon, just as "al-hasrah" (regret) and "al-wayl" (woe) are called upon. And "al-thubur": Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said it is woe (al-wayl), and al-Dahhak said it is perdition (al-halak). From it is the saying of Ibn al-Za'bara:

"When I compete with Satan in the paths of error, and whoever inclines in its inclination is ruined (mathbur)."

His saying: ﴿Do not call out﴾ through to the end of the verse means: it is said to them, in the sense of rebuke and informing them that they will abide forever: Do not limit yourselves to one grief, but grieve much, for you are deserving of that.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 25, verses 15–16:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿Say: "Is that better, or the Garden of Eternity which the God-fearing have been promised? It shall be their reward and their destination."﴾ ﴿For them therein is whatever they wish, abiding forever. It is a promise incumbent upon your Lord, one that is requested.﴾

The meaning: Say, O Muhammad, to these disbelievers who are on the path that leads to these states of the Fire: ﴿Is that better, or the Garden of Eternity?﴾ This is by way of reproach and rebuke. Since the statement is interrogative, it is permissible to use the comparative form (tafdil) between the Garden and the Fire in respect of goodness. This is because the one who asks has the right to put his interlocutor to a test about whatever he wishes, to see whether he answers correctly or wrongly. Sibawayh and others prohibit comparison between two things that share no common quality in which the comparison is made when the statement is declarative, because it involves contradiction; but when it is interrogative, that is permissible.

It has been said: the demonstrative "that" in His words "that" refers to the gardens beneath which rivers flow, and to the palaces mentioned in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Blessed is He who, if He wills, will give you﴾ [al-Furqan: 10], on the understanding that the giving is in this world. It has also been said: the demonstrative "that" refers to the treasure and the garden which the disbelievers mentioned.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The more correct view is that the demonstrative "that" in His words refers to the Fire, as we explained a little earlier.

"The God-fearing" in this verse are those who guard against shirk, for they are included in the promise; then the ranks within the promise remain according to the degrees of piety in avoiding sins.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿a promise that is requested﴾ may carry two meanings. The first, which is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd, is that it is "requested" because the believers asked for it or will ask for it. It is narrated that the angels asked God, Exalted is He, for the bounty of the God-fearing, and He promised them that. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: it is the saying of the angels, and he recited: ﴿And admit them to the Gardens of Eternity which You have promised them﴾ [Ghafir: 8]. The second meaning, mentioned by al-Tabari from some of the people of Arabic linguistics, is that it means a promise that is obligatory, one which He has made binding, so it is thereby due to be requested and demanded; and this interpretation does not imply that anyone actually requested the aforementioned promise.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 25, verse 17–19:

His saying, mighty and majestic is He:

﴿And on the Day when He gathers them, and what they worshipped besides Allah, He will say: "Did you lead these servants of Mine astray, or did they themselves stray from the way?"﴾ ﴿They will say: "Glory be to You! It was not for us to take any protectors besides You; but You gave them and their fathers enjoyment until they forgot the Reminder, and they were a people doomed to ruin."﴾ ﴿Indeed they have denied you in what you say, so you cannot avert (the punishment) nor obtain help. And whoever among you does wrong, We shall make him taste a great punishment.﴾

The meaning: "And mention the Day..." The pronoun in "yahshuruhum" refers to the disbelievers. His saying, "wa ma ya'budun" (and what they worship), intends by it everything that was worshipped besides Allah, so the expression is given the form used for non-rational beings, namely the idols, because they were the most prevalent at the time of address.

Ibn Kathir, 'Asim (in Hafs's transmission), al-A'raj and Abu Ja'far read "yahshuruhum" and "fa-yaqulu" with the ya' in both. Ibn 'Amir read them with the nun in both, which is also the reading of al-Hasan, Talha, and 'Asim as well. Nafi' read "nahshuruhum" with the nun and "fa-yaqulu" with the ya'. In the reading of 'Abd Allah: "wa ma ya'budun min dunika" (besides You). Al-A'raj read "nahshiruhum" with a kasra on the shin; this is rare in usage but strong in analogy, since "yaf'ilu" with a kasra on the ayn for transitive verbs is more analogical than "yaf'ulu" with a damma on the ayn.

This verse includes information that Allah, exalted is He, rebukes the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection by making the worshipped ones stand and address them on this meaning, so that the answer comes as disavowal of sin, and thus disgrace falls upon the disbelievers.

People differed about who answers in this verse. The majority of exegetes said: it is everyone who was worshipped from among those who have reason, such as the angels, 'Uzayr, 'Isa, and others. Al-Dahhak and 'Ikrima said: the answering entity is the idols which have no reason, which Allah, exalted is He, will empower on that day to speak this statement, and the disgrace of the disbelievers thereby becomes more complete.

The majority of readers read "nattakhidha" with a fatha on the nun, and they took the meaning to be a statement of one who has reason, and that this verse has the same meaning as the one in Surah Saba': ﴿And on the Day He gathers them all, then He will say to the angels: "Did these people worship you?"﴾ [Saba': 40] ﴿They will say: "Glory be to You! You are our Protector, not them."﴾ [Saba': 41], and like the saying of 'Isa, peace be upon him: ﴿I did not say to them except what You commanded me﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 117]. And "min awliya'" in this reading is in the position of the object. Abu Ja'far, al-Hasan, Abu al-Darda', Zayd ibn Thabit, Abu Raja', Nasr ibn 'Alqama, Makhul, Zayd ibn 'Ali, and Hafs ibn Humayd read "nuttakhadha" with a damma on the nun, and this reading follows the view of one who holds that the answering entity is the idols. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others objected that the entry of "min" in the phrase "min awliya'" weakens this reading. Abu al-Fath said: "min awliya'" is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal), and "min" entered as an extra particle because of the preceding negation, as you say: "ma ittakhadhtu Zaydan min wakil" (I did not take Zayd as an agent).

'Alqama read "ma yanbaghi" without "kana." Its retention is more appropriate in meaning, because they report a state that existed in the world, and there is no operative effect in the time of reporting.

This answerer, according to the difference of opinion concerning it, explains the aspect of the disbelievers' misguidance: how it came about, and that when Allah, exalted is He, gave them enjoyment of worldly blessings and made them abundant for them and their forefathers over long ages, they forgot the Reminder, that is, what people were reminded of through the tongues of the prophets.

"Bur" means: doomed to ruin, and al-bawar means destruction. Its form has been disputed. One group said: it is a verbal noun which is applied to both the singular and the plural, and from it is the saying of Ibn al-Za'bara:

Ya Rasul al-Malik, inna lisani rati'un ma fatafta idh ana bur

And another group said: it is the plural of ba'ir, who is one whom goodness has departed from, so that he is in the state of ruin, whether or not ruin has actually touched him afterward. al-Hasan said: the ba'ir is one in whom there is no good.

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Indeed they have denied you﴾ the verse is an address from Allah, blessed and exalted is He, without any disagreement. Whoever says "the answerer is the idols" takes its meaning to be His informing the disbelievers that their idols have denied them, and in this information there is disgrace and rebuke. The group who said "the answerer is the angels, 'Uzayr, 'Isa and the like" differed about who is addressed by this verse. One group said: the addressees are the disbelievers, by way of rebuke and reproach. Another group said: the addressees are those worshipped, Allah informing them that the disbelievers, by their ugly deeds, have denied this claim, and asserted that these are the protectors besides Allah, exalted is He. Another group said: Allah addressed the believers of the community of Muhammad ﷺ, meaning: "They have denied you, O believers, the disbelievers, in what you say of monotheism and the Law."

Ibn Kathir, Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim, and the common readers read "taqulun" with the ta' from above and "yastati'un" with the ya' from below. Abu Hatim preferred this. Abu Haywa read "yaqulun" with the ya' from below and "fa-ma tastati'un" with the ta' from above. Mujahid said: the pronoun in "yastati'un" refers to the polytheists. al-Tabari said: in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud: "fa-ma yastati'un laka sarfan," and in the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "laqad kadhdhabukum fa-ma yastati'una laka." Abu Hatim said: in the reading of 'Abd Allah: "lakum sarfan," with the pronoun in the plural.

"Sarfan" means: turning back the denial or the punishment, or whatever the meaning requires, according to the difference mentioned above.

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And whoever among you does wrong﴾ it has been said: it is an address to the disbelievers, and it has been said: it is to the believers. Wrongdoing here is polytheism, as said by al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj, though it may be understood to include other sins. In Ubayy's reading: "wa man yakdhib minkum nudhqhu 'adhaban alima" (And whoever among you lies, We shall make him taste a painful punishment).

Mujahid said: the pronoun in "yastati'un" refers to the polytheists. al-Tabari said: in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud: "fa-ma yastati'un laka sarfan," and in the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "laqad kadhdhabukum fa-ma yastati'una laka." Abu Hatim said: in the reading of 'Abd Allah: "lakum sarfan," with the pronoun in the plural.

"Sarfan" means: turning back the denial or the punishment, or whatever the meaning requires, according to the difference mentioned above.

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And whoever among you does wrong﴾ it has been said: it is an address to the disbelievers, and it has been said: it is to the believers. Wrongdoing here is polytheism, as said by al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj, though it may be understood to include other sins. In Ubayy's reading: "wa man yakdhib minkum nudhqhu 'adhaban alima" (And whoever among you lies, We shall make him taste a painful punishment).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 25, verses 20–21:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿We never sent before you any messengers but that they ate food and walked in the markets. And We made some of you a trial for others. Will you be patient? And your Lord is ever Seeing.﴾ ﴿And those who do not expect to meet Us say: "Why have the angels not been sent down to us, or why do we not see our Lord?" Indeed, they have become arrogant within themselves and have transgressed with great transgression.﴾

This verse is a refutation of the disbelievers of Quraysh, who found it implausible that a messenger should be from among mankind, and of their saying: ﴿What is this messenger that he eats food and walks in the markets?﴾ [al-Furqan: 7]. Allah the Exalted informed Muhammad (ﷺ) and his community that He had not sent any prophet before him in the bygone ages except with this attribute.

On this elided, presumed object, the pronoun in His saying "innahum" (indeed they) refers back. A group went to the view that His saying ﴿they eat food﴾ is a metonymy for the occurrence of the natural need (ḥadath).

The majority of readers read "wa-yamshūna" (and they walk) with a fatḥa on the yā' (ya), sukūn on the mīm, and a light shīn. ʿAlī, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān and Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with them, read "wa-yumashshawna" with a ḍamma on the yā', a fatḥa on the mīm, and a doubled shīn with fatḥa, meaning: they call to walking and compel others to it. Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān read with a ḍamma on the yā', a fatḥa on the mīm, and a ḍamma on the doubled shīn, and it has the same meaning as "yamshūna" (they walk). From this is the saying of the poet:

"Umashshī bi-aʿṭān al-miyāh wa-abtaghī / qalāʾiṣ minhā ṣaʿbatun wa-rakūb"
(I walk among the watering-places of the waters, seeking from them she-camels that are difficult and yet rideable.)

Then He, blessed and exalted, informed that the cause of this is that He, glory be to Him, willed to make some of His servants a trial for others in general, across all people, believer and disbeliever alike. So the healthy person is a trial for the sick, the wealthy a trial for the poor, the grateful poor a trial for the wealthy, and the messenger singled out with the honour of prophethood a trial for the noble disbelievers of his age. Likewise the scholars and the just rulers. Ibn al-Qasim recited this verse when he saw Ashhab. The reproach in ﴿Will you be patient?﴾ is specific to the true believers, and so it addresses the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). It is as if He made the respite given to the disbelievers a trial for the believers, that is, a test for them; then He put them on notice: will you be patient or not? Then His saying ﴿And your Lord is ever Seeing﴾ implies a promise to the patient and a threat to the disobedient.

Then He informed of the saying of the disbelievers: ﴿Why have the angels not been sent down to us?﴾, and so on to the end of the verse. His saying, the Exalted, "yarjūna" (they expect): Abū ʿUbayda and a people said its meaning is: they fear. The evidence for this is the saying of the Hudhalī:

"Idhā lasaʿathu al-naḥlu lam yarju lasʿahā / wa-khālafahā fī bayti nawbin ʿawāmil"
(When the bee stings him, he does not expect its sting [to be averted], and he opposes it in a house of… workers.)

The Qadi Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What appears to me is that "rajāʾ" (hope) in the verse and the line is in its proper sense, because fear of meeting Allah the Exalted is always coupled with hope in Him. So when hope is negated for someone, He has only informed that he denies the Resurrection, since fear and hope are both negated. In mentioning the disbelievers with the negation of hope there is an alert to the great loss of what they have missed of hoping in Allah the Exalted. As for the line of poetry mentioned, its meaning to me is: he does not hope to repel it nor to be freed from it; therefore he endures patiently and strives diligently in his occupation.

When the disbelievers of Quraysh wished to see their Lord, the Exalted informed of them that they magnified themselves and asked for what they were not worthy of. "ʿAtaw" means: they were stubborn against the truth and became fierce. It is said ʿitiyy and ʿutuww: ʿutuww according to the original form, and ʿitiyy because the ḍamma on the wāw was deemed heavy, so it was changed to a yā', then the letter before it was kasra-ed, seeking harmony.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 25, verses 22–26:**

The Most High said:

﴿On the day they see the angels, there will be no good news that day for the guilty; and they will say, "A forbidden barrier."﴾ ﴿And We will turn to whatever deeds they did and make them scattered dust.﴾ ﴿The companions of the Garden, that day, will have a better resting place and a finer place of rest.﴾ ﴿And the day the sky will be split open with clouds, and the angels will be sent down in a descent.﴾ ﴿The true sovereignty that day belongs to the Most Merciful, and it will be a difficult day for the disbelievers.﴾

The meaning of this verse is that when the disbelievers said, ﴿Why have the angels not been sent down upon us?﴾ [al-Furqan: 21], what they meant was the Day of Resurrection. The beginning of the verse could allow the reading that it refers to the day their souls depart, but its end requires that the reference is to the Day of Resurrection. The grammatical governance of these time expressions (al-'awamil, the governing words) is clear to anyone who reflects on it, so we have summarised it for that reason. The meaning of the verse is: those who wished for the descent of the angels do not know what God the Exalted has decreed in this matter. On the day they see the angels, it will be an evil for them and not good news. Rather, for them there is loss and the encounter with what is hateful. On that day there is no good and no good news, because time expressions are a report about their sources (al-masadir, the verbal nouns they govern).

As for the pronoun in His saying "and they will say," al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Dahhak and Mujahid said that it refers to "the angels." The meaning is: the angels will say to the guilty, "A forbidden barrier; good news is forbidden to you," that is, a prohibited and forbidden thing. From this is the verse of Jarir ibn 'Abd al-Masih:

*"The far palm tree yearned for me, so I said to it: a forbidden barrier, unlawful; is that not the Dahariyas?"*

Mujahid also said, as did Ibn Jurayj, that the pronoun in His saying "and they will say" refers to the guilty disbelievers. Ibn Jurayj said: when the Arabs disliked something, they would say "hijran." Mujahid said: "hijran" means "awdhan" (a protection), they seek refuge with the angels.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

It is possible that the meaning is: they will say, "A forbidden, prohibited thing for us is pardon." Abu 'Ubaydah mentioned that these two words are a formula of protection among the Arabs, said by one who fears another within the sacred precinct, or in a sacred month, when he meets him while there is a blood-feud between them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This meaning is the intent of the verse of al-Mutalammis that has preceded, that is: that which she yearned for is forbidden.

(p-430) Al-Hasan and Abu Raja' read "hujran" with a damma on the ha', while the people read it with a kasra.

Then He, the Most High, informed of what His judgment and action will bring, and He said, relating about the Day of Resurrection: "and We will turn," that is, Our judgment and execution will be directed (qasada hukmuna wa infadhuna). Words similar to this are appropriate. It was also said that it is the arrival of the angels, and He attributed it to Himself because it is by His command. The expression "qadimna" (We turned) is apt because one who comes upon something hateful has not settled it, nor has he commanded it, so the one who changes it and removes it is the one who arrives at it. As for the saying of the rajiz (the rajaz poet):

*"The misguided Kharijites came, to the servants of our Lord, and said: indeed your blood is lawful for us."*

Here "qudum" retains its basic meaning (arrival).

The meaning of the verse is: We turn to their deeds, which in reality weigh nothing, since there is no intention with them. We make them, according to what they deserve, as things that are not counted, and We make them scattered dust, that is, a thing with no benefit. The "haba'" (fine dust) is the tiny particles dispersed in the air, which cannot be perceived by the senses except when the sun enters a narrow place surrounded by shadow, like an aperture or the like. Then there appear in the place opposite the sun things that vanish and appear. That is the haba'. Its description in this verse as "scattered" (mansur) and in another verse as "dispersed" (munbath): one group said they are the same. Another group said that "munbath" is finer and more subtle than "mansur," because "mansur" implies that something else scattered it, such as the hooves of horses, winds, or the demolition of a wall and the like, while "munbath" is as if it was dispersed by its own fineness. Others said: "haba' mansur" is what the winds blow and scatter. It is reported from one of them that he said: "haba'" is poured-out water. The first is more correct. The Arabs say: "habbat al-ghubar" and the like when it scatters the dust. The poet said:

*"You see behind it, from the dust and the sand, a flurry like a mirage."*

(p-432) The meaning of this verse: We made their deeds without judgment and without standing.

Then the Mighty and Majestic informed that the resting place of the people of the Garden is better than the resting place of the people of the Fire. "Khayr" (better) here is used for comparison between two things that have no sharing between them. Al-Zajjaj and others said: since the two share the fact that this is a resting place and this is a resting place, He preferred one resting place.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

It appears to me that these expressions, which contain a general sense and whose judgment applies from various aspects, such as your saying "ahabb" (more beloved), "ahsan" (finer), "khayr" (better), and "sharr" (worse), may be used between two things that share nothing. So you say: happiness in this world is more beloved to me than misery. That is, there may be found, in some respect, one who prefers misery, such as the ascetic worshipper or the one who is angered. Likewise in other cases. So when "af'al" (the comparative form) has the meaning that one of the two things has no share in it in any respect, then the report of preference with it is invalid, as in your saying: water is colder than fire. From this is that you say of a ruby and a clod of earth (and you point to the clod): this is better and finer and more beloved and superior to that. If you said: this is brighter and more radiant than that, it would be invalid.

As for His saying "maqilan" (resting place): Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, al-Nakha'i and Ibn Jurayj held that the reckoning of creation will be completed at the time of the height of the day, and the resting place (maqil) of the people of the Garden is in the Garden, and the people of the Fire in the Fire. So "maqil" is from "qayla" (the midday rest).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

It is possible that the word only includes the preference of the Garden as a whole and the goodness of its air. The Arabs prefer lands for the goodness of their midday rest, since at the time of the qayla the badness of a land's air becomes apparent. So if a land is good at the time when the air is bad, the preference is valid. From this is the saying of al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur al-Iyadi:

*"A land chosen for the goodness of its resting place, by Ka'b ibn Mamah and Ibn Umm Du'ad."*

His saying, the Most High: ﴿And the day the sky is split﴾ means the Day of Resurrection, at the time when the sky is rent asunder, the angels descend, and the recompense takes place with the reality of the reckoning. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "tashsha'aqqaqu" with the shin and the qaf both doubled. The rest read it with a single shin. His saying "bil-ghamam" means it is split open from it, and "al-ghamam" is a thin, white, beautiful cloud, which no human has seen yet, except what came in the shading of the Children of Israel. The majority of readers recited "wa nuzzila al-mala'ikatu tanzilan," with a damma on the nun, a shadda on the zay with a kasra, and the "al-mala'ikatu" in the nominative as a passive subject (maf'ul lam yusamma fa'iluh). Abu 'Amr, in the transmission of 'Abd al-Wahhab, read "wa nuzila," with the zay with a kasra and no shadda. Abu al-Fath said: this is not well known, because "nuzila" is not transitive to an object, so that it is passive here for "al-mala'ikah." Its explanation is that it is like "zukima al-rajulu wa junna" (the man was afflicted with a cold and became insane), for it is only said "azkamahu Allah wa ajannahu" (God afflicted him with a cold and made him insane). This is a matter of transmission (sama'), not analogy (qiyas). Abu Raja' read "wa nazzala" with a fatha on the nun and a shadda on the zay. Al-A'mash read "wa anzala al-mala'ikata," and Ibn Mas'ud likewise read it. Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "wa nazalati al-mala'ikatu." Ibn Kathir alone read "wa nunazzilu al-mala'ikata" with two nuns, and this is the reading of the people of Makkah; it was also related from Abu 'Amr. Harun reported from Abu 'Amr: "wa nazzala al-mala'ikatu," attributing the verb to them. A group read "wa yanzilu al-mala'ikatu," and Ubayy ibn Ka'b also read "wa tanazzalati al-mala'ikatu."

He determined that the true sovereignty on that day belongs to the Most Merciful, since every sovereignty has passed away on that day. Its difficulty for the disbelievers is explained by the Fire entering upon them on that day, and by what occurs during it of frightful things. His saying, ﴿for the disbelievers﴾, is evidence that this day is easy for the believers. It is related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Indeed God, the Most High, will make the Day of Resurrection easy for the believer, until it is lighter for him than an obligatory prayer that he prayed in the world."

As for His saying "maqilan" (resting place): Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, al-Nakha'i and Ibn Jurayj held that the reckoning of creation will be completed at the time of the height of the day, and the resting place (maqil) of the people of the Garden is in the Garden, and the people of the Fire in the Fire. So "maqil" is from "qayla" (the midday rest).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

It is possible that the word only includes the preference of the Garden as a whole and the goodness of its air. The Arabs prefer lands for the goodness of their midday rest, since at the time of the qayla the badness of a land's air becomes apparent. So if a land is good at the time when the air is bad, the preference is valid. From this is the saying of al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur al-Iyadi:

*"A land chosen for the goodness of its resting place, by Ka'b ibn Mamah and Ibn Umm Du'ad."*

His saying, the Most High: ﴿And the day the sky is split﴾ means the Day of Resurrection, at the time when the sky is rent asunder, the angels descend, and the recompense takes place with the reality of the reckoning. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "tashsha'aqqaqu" with the shin and the qaf both doubled. The rest read it with a single shin. His saying "bil-ghamam" means it is split open from it, and "al-ghamam" is a thin, white, beautiful cloud, which no human has seen yet, except what came in the shading of the Children of Israel. The majority of readers recited "wa nuzzila al-mala'ikatu tanzilan," with a damma on the nun, a shadda on the zay with a kasra, and the "al-mala'ikatu" in the nominative as a passive subject (maf'ul lam yusamma fa'iluh). Abu 'Amr, in the transmission of 'Abd al-Wahhab, read "wa nuzila," with the zay with a kasra and no shadda. Abu al-Fath said: this is not well known, because "nuzila" is not transitive to an object, so that it is passive here for "al-mala'ikah." Its explanation is that it is like "zukima al-rajulu wa junna" (the man was afflicted with a cold and became insane), for it is only said "azkamahu Allah wa ajannahu" (God afflicted him with a cold and made him insane). This is a matter of transmission (sama'), not analogy (qiyas). Abu Raja' read "wa nazzala" with a fatha on the nun and a shadda on the zay. Al-A'mash read "wa anzala al-mala'ikata," and Ibn Mas'ud likewise read it. Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "wa nazalati al-mala'ikatu." Ibn Kathir alone read "wa nunazzilu al-mala'ikata" with two nuns, and this is the reading of the people of Makkah; it was also related from Abu 'Amr. Harun reported from Abu 'Amr: "wa nazzala al-mala'ikatu," attributing the verb to them. A group read "wa yanzilu al-mala'ikatu," and Ubayy ibn Ka'b also read "wa tanazzalati al-mala'ikatu."

He determined that the true sovereignty on that day belongs to the Most Merciful, since every sovereignty has passed away on that day. Its difficulty for the disbelievers is explained by the Fire entering upon them on that day, and by what occurs during it of frightful things. His saying, ﴿for the disbelievers﴾, is evidence that this day is easy for the believers. It is related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Indeed God, the Most High, will make the Day of Resurrection easy for the believer, until it is lighter for him than an obligatory prayer that he prayed in the world."

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And on the Day the wrongdoer will bite his hands, saying, "Oh, I wish I had taken a way with the Messenger."﴾ ﴿"Woe to me! I wish I had not taken so-and-so as a friend.﴾ ﴿He had led me astray from the Reminder after it had come to me. And Satan is ever, to man, a deserter."﴾ ﴿And the Messenger will say, "My Lord, indeed my people have taken this Qur'an as something abandoned."﴾ ﴿And thus We have made for every prophet an enemy among the criminals. And sufficient is your Lord as guide and helper.﴾

"Yawm" (the day) is an adverbial object (ẓarf), and its governing verb is an implied verb. "Biting the hands" is the action of one who is regretful, distressed and lamenting. Ibn 'Abbas and a group of the exegetes said: "The wrongdoer" in this verse is 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt; that is because he had embraced Islam or inclined towards Islam, and Ubayy ibn Khalaf, whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) killed with his own hand on the Day of Uhud, was a close friend of 'Uqba. So he forbade him from Islam, and he obeyed his prohibition, and the verse was revealed concerning the two of them. Thus the wrongdoer is 'Uqba, and "so-and-so" is Ubayy. In some narrations from Ibn 'Abbas, the wrongdoer is Ubayy, for he used to come to the Prophet (ﷺ), and 'Uqba forbade him, and he obeyed him.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Whoever includes Umayya ibn Khalaf in this verse has erred, except according to the opinion of one who regards "the wrongdoer" as a generic noun (ism jins).

Mujahid and Abu Raja' said: "The wrongdoer" is a generic noun, and "so-and-so" is Satan.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It appears that "the wrongdoer" is general, and that the purpose of the verse is to magnify a day on which the wrongdoers disown their intimate companions who commanded them to do wrong. Since the close friend of each wrongdoer is other than the close friend of another, and each wrongdoer names a specific man for himself, He expressed that by "so-and-so," which carries the complete generality, and its meaning is common among people. There is no wrongdoer except that in his worldly life he has a close friend who helps him and incites him; this is generally the case. It seems that the cause of the verse and the arrangement of these meanings was 'Uqba and Ubayy. His saying "with the Messenger" strengthens this, by making the definiteness of "the Messenger" refer to a specific one, indicating Muhammad (ﷺ). On the first interpretation, the definiteness is generic.

All of them recited "layti" with a silent yā’, except Abu 'Amr, who vocalised the yā’ in "laytanī ittakhadhtu" ("layti" with a vowel). Abu Hamid narrated from Nafi' the same as Abu 'Amr. The "sabīl" (way) that is wished for is the way of the Hereafter. In this verse there is a warning to every person of understanding to avoid the evil companion, and the hadiths and wise sayings on this subject are numerous and well known.

His, the Exalted, saying: "Ya waylatā" — the tā’ in it is a substitute for the yā’ in "yā waylī," and the alif is that which is in their saying "yā ghulāman," and it is a dialect. A group recited "yā waylatā" with imāla (inclination of the alif), and Abu 'Ali said: (p-436) Leaving off the imāla is better, because the original of this word is the yā’: "yā waylatay," then the kasra was changed to a fatha and the yā’ to an alif, fleeing from the yā’. Whoever uses imāla returns to what he fled from initially.

"Dhikr" is that by which a person is reminded of the matter of his Hereafter, whether Qur'an, admonition or the like. "And Satan is ever, to man, a deserter" may be from the saying of the wrongdoer, and it may be a beginning, an information from Allah, Exalted, by way of indicating the nature of their error and warning against Satan, who had reached that extent.

His, the Exalted, saying: "And the Messenger will say" is a report of the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in this world, complaining of what he suffers from his people. This is the view of the majority and is the apparent one. Another group said: it is a report of his saying in the Hereafter. Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited "qawmī" with a vowelled yā’, while the rest recited it with a silent yā’. "Mahjūran" may mean: distanced and cast away; [and it may be] from the "hujr" (with a damma on the hā’), indicating their saying: poetry, soothsaying and magic. This is the view of Mujahid and al-Nakha'i.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Ibn Zayd says: it is an admonition to the believers to keep constant with the mushaf, and not to let dust cover it in the houses while one is occupied with other things. Anas narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever hangs up a mushaf and does not attend to it will come on the Day of Resurrection clinging to it, saying: 'This has taken me as something abandoned. Judge, O Lord, between me and him.'"

Then He consoled him regarding the deeds of his people by informing him that other messengers before him were likewise tested with enemies in their time; that is, be patient as they were patient, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. "'Aduwwan" is used to mean the plural (p-437), as you say: "These are an enemy to me," describing with it the plural, the singular and the feminine. Then He, the Exalted, promised him with His saying: "And sufficient is your Lord as guide and helper." The "bi" in "bi-rabbika" is for emphasis, indicating the meaning, which is: be content with your Lord.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Whoever includes Umayya ibn Khalaf in this verse has erred, except according to the opinion of one who regards "the wrongdoer" as a generic noun (ism jins).

Mujahid and Abu Raja' said: "The wrongdoer" is a generic noun, and "so-and-so" is Satan.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It appears that "the wrongdoer" is general, and that the purpose of the verse is to magnify a day on which the wrongdoers disown their intimate companions who commanded them to do wrong. Since the close friend of each wrongdoer is other than the close friend of another, and each wrongdoer names a specific man for himself, He expressed that by "so-and-so," which carries the complete generality, and its meaning is common among people. There is no wrongdoer except that in his worldly life he has a close friend who helps him and incites him; this is generally the case. It seems that the cause of the verse and the arrangement of these meanings was 'Uqba and Ubayy. His saying "with the Messenger" strengthens this, by making the definiteness of "the Messenger" refer to a specific one, indicating Muhammad (ﷺ). On the first interpretation, the definiteness is generic.

All of them recited "layti" with a silent yā’, except Abu 'Amr, who vocalised the yā’ in "laytanī ittakhadhtu" ("layti" with a vowel). Abu Hamid narrated from Nafi' the same as Abu 'Amr. The "sabīl" (way) that is wished for is the way of the Hereafter. In this verse there is a warning to every person of understanding to avoid the evil companion, and the hadiths and wise sayings on this subject are numerous and well known.

His, the Exalted, saying: "Ya waylatā" — the tā’ in it is a substitute for the yā’ in "yā waylī," and the alif is that which is in their saying "yā ghulāman," and it is a dialect. A group recited "yā waylatā" with imāla (inclination of the alif), and Abu 'Ali said: (p-436) Leaving off the imāla is better, because the original of this word is the yā’: "yā waylatay," then the kasra was changed to a fatha and the yā’ to an alif, fleeing from the yā’. Whoever uses imāla returns to what he fled from initially.

"Dhikr" is that by which a person is reminded of the matter of his Hereafter, whether Qur'an, admonition or the like. "And Satan is ever, to man, a deserter" may be from the saying of the wrongdoer, and it may be a beginning, an information from Allah, Exalted, by way of indicating the nature of their error and warning against Satan, who had reached that extent.

His, the Exalted, saying: "And the Messenger will say" is a report of the saying of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in this world, complaining of what he suffers from his people. This is the view of the majority and is the apparent one. Another group said: it is a report of his saying in the Hereafter. Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited "qawmī" with a vowelled yā’, while the rest recited it with a silent yā’. "Mahjūran" may mean: distanced and cast away; [and it may be] from the "hujr" (with a damma on the hā’), indicating their saying: poetry, soothsaying and magic. This is the view of Mujahid and al-Nakha'i.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Ibn Zayd says: it is an admonition to the believers to keep constant with the mushaf, and not to let dust cover it in the houses while one is occupied with other things. Anas narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever hangs up a mushaf and does not attend to it will come on the Day of Resurrection clinging to it, saying: 'This has taken me as something abandoned. Judge, O Lord, between me and him.'"

Then He consoled him regarding the deeds of his people by informing him that other messengers before him were likewise tested with enemies in their time; that is, be patient as they were patient, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. "'Aduwwan" is used to mean the plural (p-437), as you say: "These are an enemy to me," describing with it the plural, the singular and the feminine. Then He, the Exalted, promised him with His saying: "And sufficient is your Lord as guide and helper." The "bi" in "bi-rabbika" is for emphasis, indicating the meaning, which is: be content with your Lord.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 25, verses 32–34:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And those who disbelieve say: "Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?" Thus [it is], that We may strengthen your heart thereby, and We have recited it in measured recitation.﴾ ﴿And they do not bring you any example but that We bring you the truth and the better explanation.﴾ ﴿Those who will be gathered upon their faces to Hell—those are worse in position and further astray in way.﴾

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and others, that the disbelievers of Quraysh said, in some of their objections: "If this Qur'an were from Allah, the Exalted, it would have been sent down all at once, as the Torah and the Gospel were sent down." His saying ﴿Thus﴾ may be from the speech of the disbelievers, [and it may be a resumed statement from the speech of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, not from their speech], and this is more preferable. Its meaning is: "As it was sent down, We willed it," so the reference is to its being sent down in installments. Allah, the Exalted, made the cause of its being sent down in installments over time the strengthening of the heart of Muhammad ﷺ and that he might memorise it. Makki and al-Rummani said: Since he was unlettered and could not write, and so that it would correspond to the occasions that arose at their times, it was sent down over a little more than twenty years, whereas the other messengers could write, so it was sent down all at once. 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, recited "liyuthabbita" with a ya'. "Tartil" (measured recitation) means separating things that follow one another; from it comes their saying "baqar ratil" (cattle with separated teeth), and from it comes "tartil al-qira'a" (measured recitation of the Qur'an). Allah, Blessed and Exalted, willed that the Qur'an be sent down in the events and incidents that He had decreed, and decreed its descent for them.

Then Allah, the Exalted, informed His Prophet that these disbelievers do not bring any vague example, [which they set forth by way of objection]—such as their comparison in this case with the Torah and the Gospel—except that the Qur'an came with the truth regarding it, meaning with that which is true; then it is "better in explanation," or clearer in exposition and detail. Then Allah, the Exalted, threatened the disbelievers with what will befall them on the Day of Resurrection: being gathered upon their faces into the Fire. The majority held that this walking upon the faces is literal, and it was narrated concerning this—by way of Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him—(p-438) a hadith that a man said to the Prophet ﷺ: "O Messenger of Allah, how will they be able to walk upon their faces?" He said: "Indeed, the One who made them able to walk upon their feet is able to make them walk upon their faces." And a group said: walking upon the faces is a metaphor for extreme humiliation, abasement and disgrace. His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿worse in position﴾: the discussion of it is like the discussion of His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿better as an abode﴾ [al-Furqan: 24].

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 25, verses 35–39:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book and appointed with him his brother Aaron as a minister.﴾ ﴿Then We said, "Go to the people who denied Our signs," so We destroyed them with complete destruction.﴾ ﴿And the people of Noah, when they denied the messengers, We drowned them and made them a sign for mankind. And We have prepared for the wrongdoers a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿And [We destroyed] 'Ad and Thamud and the companions of the Rass, and many generations between them.﴾ ﴿And to each We presented examples, and each We destroyed with complete destruction.﴾

These verses in which the nations are mentioned are an illustration for them (the disbelievers of Makkah) and a warning that there will befall them what befell those who were punished.

"Al-Kitab" (the Book) is the Torah. "Al-wazir" (the minister) is the helper; it derives from tahammul al-wizr (bearing a burden), i.e., the weight of a situation, and from al-wazar (refuge, shelter).

"The people who denied" (﴿al-qawm alladhina kadhdhabu﴾) are Pharaoh and his chiefs from the Copts. Then much was omitted from the speech, which is indicated by what remains. The estimated omitted part is: "So they both went, delivered the message, and they denied them, so We destroyed them."

'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, and Maslama ibn Muharib read: "fa-dammiranni-hum" (so be the cause of that). Abu al-Fath said: he attached the nun of emphasis to the dual alif of the dual, as you say to a man: "idribanni Zaydan" (strike Zayd).

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him: "fa-dammiraa-hum." Abu 'Amr al-Dani reported from them: "fa-damirna-hum" with a light kasra on the mim. He said: It is also related from them: "fa-dammiru bihim" in the imperative for a group, with an added ba'. What Abu al-Fath explained is a mistake; the reading is actually "fa-dammiru bihim" with the ba', and al-Mahdawi also mentioned it thus.

The word "qawm" (people) is in the accusative by a hidden verb indicated by "aghraqnahum." His saying, "al-Rusul" (the messengers), although they denied only Noah, means that a community which denies one prophet, in that is included the denial of all the prophets. So the expression came with what their action implied, as a figure of speech in describing them. His saying, "ayah" (a sign), means a sign of the might of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, for every disbeliever in His prophets.

"Ad and Thamud" are inflected and not inflected. Here it came inflected. Ibn Mas'ud, 'Amr ibn Maymun, al-Hasan and 'Isa read "wa-'Adan" inflected, and "Thamuda" uninflected.

People differed about "Ashab al-Rass" (the companions of the Rass). Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: they are a people from Thamud. Qatadah said: the people of a village from Yamamah called al-Rass. Ka'b, Muqatil and al-Suddi said: al-Rass is a well at Antioch of Syria, in which the companion of Ya-Sin was killed. al-Kalbi said: the companions of the Rass are a people to whom a prophet was sent and they killed him. Qatadah said: the companions of the Rass and the companions of the Thicket (al-Aykah) are two peoples to whom Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, was sent; and Wahb ibn Munabbih said the same. 'Ali, in the book of al-Tha'labi, said: the companions of the Rass are a people who worshipped a pine tree called "Shah Darakht," and they buried their prophet in a well, or a grave, or a mine. From this is the saying of the poet:

"You outran with a band of Tanabilah a forerunner, digging the rissas."

'Ikrimah and Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi related from the Prophet ﷺ that the people of the Rass mentioned in this verse are a people who seized their prophet, threw him into a well, and closed over him a rock. There was a black slave who believed in him; he would bring food to that well, and Allah would help him against that rock, so he would lift it, and he, believing in that prophet, would give him what nourished him; then he would return the rock. Until Allah made that black slave sleep for fourteen years. And the people of the village brought out their prophet and they believed in him... in a long hadith. Al-Tabari said: it is possible that they disbelieved in him after that, so Allah mentioned them in this verse.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He, "and many generations between them": it is an indefinite expression whose reality none knows except Allah. The explanation of "qarn" (generation) and how many it is has already been given. From this wording the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is related to have said, as is narrated (and it is related that Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said it): "The genealogists have lied about what is above 'Adnan," because Allah, Blessed and Exalted, informed about many nations and creatures and did not inform about others.

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: indeed for each of these He set forth examples so that he might be guided, but he was not guided; so Allah destroyed him (tabbarahu), i.e., caused him to perish. "Al-tabar" is destruction, and "al-tibr" is gold, i.e., that which is broken and crushed; and for this reason the crumbs of marble and glass are called "tibr." Ibn Jubayr said: the origin of the word is Nabataean, but the Arabs have used it.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 25, verses 48–52**

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And it is He who sends the winds as good tidings before His mercy, and We send down from the sky pure water,﴾ ﴿that We may give life thereby to a dead land and give it to drink, of what We have created, cattle and many people.﴾ ﴿And We have certainly distributed it among them that they may remember, but most of the people refuse except ingratitude.﴾ ﴿And had We willed, We would have sent a warner to every town.﴾ ﴿So do not obey the disbelievers, and strive against them with it, a great striving.﴾

One group recited "al-riyah" (الرِياحَ, the winds, plural), and another group recited "al-rih" (الرِيحَ, the wind, singular) as a collective noun (jins), so it has the meaning of "al-riyah." We have mentioned this recitation (qira'a) in the commentary on Surah al-A'raf. The plural reading is preferable, because the established usage of "al-rih" (الرِيحِ) whenever it appears in the Qur'an in the singular is for punishment, and whenever it is for rain and mercy it is in the plural "riyah." This is because the wind of rain is dispersed, scattered, comes gently from here and there, and one after another, whereas the wind of punishment is violent and does not scatter; it comes as a single body. Do you not see that it smashes what it finds and destroys it? Al-Rummani said: "The winds of mercy are plural because they are three fertilizing winds: the south wind, the east wind, and the north wind. The wind of punishment is singular because it is one wind that does not fertilize, and it is the west wind."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

"This is challenged by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) when the wind blew: «O Allah, make them winds (riyahan) and do not make them a wind (rihan).»" The readers differed concerning "al-nashr" (النَشْرِ, dispersal) in the letters nun and ba' and otherwise, a difference we have mentioned in the commentary on Surah al-A'raf. "Nashran" means "spreading out and scattered."

"Al-tahur" (الطَهُورُ) is an intensive form (bina' mubalagha) of "tahir" (pure). This intensity requires that the water of the sky, and everything that comes from it and is connected to it, be pure and purifying. He described the land as "dead" (maytan), because He made it like the verbal noun (masdar) which is used to describe the masculine and feminine alike; this is permissible because "balda" has the meaning of "balad."

Talha ibn Musarrif recited "linunshi'a bihi baldatan maytan wa nunsiqahu" (لِنُنْشِئَ بِهِ بَلْدَةً مَيْتًا ونُسْقِيَهُ) with a damma on the nun, and this is the recitation of the majority (jumhur). Its meaning: We make it a drink (suqya) for them. This is the view of some linguists regarding "asqa," who said that "saqa" means giving drink to the lips. The majority said "saqa" and "asqa" have the same meaning, and a verse of Labid is cited as evidence:

"Saqa qawmi Bani Majdin wa asqa Numayran wal-qaba'ila min Hilal."

Abu 'Amr recited "nasqiyahu" (نَسْقِيَهُ) with a fatha on the nun, and this is the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abi 'Absa, Abu Haywa, and it is narrated from Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him.

"Anasi" (أناسِيَّ): it is said to be the plural of "insan" (human), and the doubled ya' is a substitute for the nun in the singular. This is the view of Sibawayh. Al-Mubarrad said it is the plural of "insi" (إنسِيّ), so the analogical form would have been "anasiyah," as they said of "muhalabbi" (مُهْلَّبِيٌّ): "mahalibah." Al-Tabari related from some linguists that the plural of "insan" is "anasin" with a nun, like "sarhan" and "bustan." Yahya ibn al-Harith recited "anasiya" (أناسِيَ) with the ya' lightened.

The pronoun in "sarrafnahu" (صَرَّفْناهُ) refers, according to Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid, to the water sent down from the sky. The meaning is that Allah, blessed and exalted, made the sending down of water a reminder for them, by directing it from some places to others, and it is all in every year in one measure. This is also said by Ibn Mas'ud. According to this interpretation, His saying: ﴿But most of the people refuse except ingratitude﴾ means in their saying that rain is due to the "anwa'" (stars' risings) and the planets, as said by Ikrima. It is also said that "kufuran" is general, since they abandoned remembrance.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: the pronoun in "sarrafnahu" refers to the Qur'an, even though it has not been mentioned before, because the matter is clear. This is strengthened by His saying after it: ﴿and strive against them with it﴾. According to the first interpretation, the pronoun in "bihi" (with it) is intended to refer to the Qur'an, in the manner we have mentioned. Ibn Zayd said: it is intended to refer to Islam.

Ikrima recited "sarafnahu" (صَرَفْناهُ) with the ra' lightened. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and the Kufans recited "liyadhkurū" (لِيَذْكُرُوا) with the dhal sukun, and the rest recited "liyadhdhakkarū" (لِيَذَّكَّرُوا) with the dhal and kaf doubled.

In His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And had We willed﴾, the verse is an abbreviation (iqtida'), indicated by what we have mentioned. Its supposed completion is: "But We chose you, singled you out and preferred you, so do not obey the disbelievers."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 25, verse 53–57:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And it is He who let loose the two seas, one sweet and palatable, and the other salty and bitter; and He placed between them a barrier and an inviolable partition.﴾ ﴿And it is He who created from water a human being and made him [a relative by] lineage and marriage. And your Lord is ever Powerful.﴾ ﴿And they worship, besides Allah, that which neither benefits them nor harms them. And the disbeliever is ever a helper [of Satan] against his Lord.﴾ ﴿And We have not sent you except as a bringer of good news and a warner.﴾ ﴿Say, "I do not ask you for it any payment, except that whoever wills may take to his Lord a way."﴾

The people have differed in the interpretation of this verse. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him both) said: he meant the sea of the sky and the sea that is on the earth, and the wording of the verse is arranged accordingly. Mujahid said: the sweet sea is the waters of the rivers that fall into the salty sea, and their falling into it is its "mixing" (marj). He said: the barrier (barzakh) and the partition (hijr) is a barrier in the knowledge of Allah the Exalted which humans do not see, and al-Zajjaj said the same. A group said: the meaning of "maraja" is that He continued one of them within the other. Ibn 'Abbas also said: He made one of them prevail over the other. And other sayings of this kind, which are many.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

What I say concerning the verse is that its purpose is to draw attention to the power of Allah the Exalted and the perfection of His creation of things, in that He spread through the earth abundant sweet waters from rivers, springs and wells, and placed them amidst the salty water, and placed the salty water amidst them. So you see the sea surrounded by sweet waters on its two banks, and you find the water in the sea, at the islands and the like, surrounded by salty water. Thus He dispersed them in this way across the earth; "mixing" (kh alt) them is what is meant, and from it is His saying "maraja", and from it [comes] ﴿in a confused matter﴾ [Qaf: 5].

"The two seas" refers to all the sweet water and all the salty water, as if He said: He let loose the two kinds of water. So the barrier and the partition are what lies between the two seas of land and dry ground, as al-Hasan said. And from it is the power that holds them apart despite their closeness in some places. All the people read "hijr" here with a kasra on the ha', while al-Hasan read it with a damma on the ha' throughout the Qur'an. "Barzakh" is the barrier between two things.

Talhah ibn Musarrif read "wa-hadha malih" (with fatha on the mim and kasra on the lam), while the majority read "hadha milh" (with kasra on the mim). Abu Hatim said: this is an unusual reading. Ibn Jinni said: he meant "malih" (salty), and dropped the alif, as in "'ard" and "bard". And "ujaj" is the most intense degree of saltiness.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And it is He who created from water a human being﴾ to the end of the verse. It is an enumeration of the blessing upon people in bringing them into existence after non-existence, and a drawing of attention to the lesson in that, and an enumeration of the blessing in the bond between them of lineage and marriage. His saying "from water" may either mean the origin of creation, in that every living thing is created from water, or it may mean the sperm of men, and a group said each of these. The first is more eloquent and clearer. "Lineage (nasab) and marriage (sihr)" are two meanings that encompass every kinship that exists between any two human beings. Lineage is that a person and another share a father or a mother, whether that kinship is near or distant. Marriage is the bond of matrimonial alliance; the relatives of the wife are the *akhtan*, and the relatives of the husband are the *ahma'*; and *al-asbar* is a general term for all of that. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) said: lineage is what marriage to is forbidden, and marriage is what marriage to is permitted. Al-Dahhak said: marriage is kinship through nursing.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

In my view, this is a mistake caused by the fact that Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) said: "Seven are forbidden by lineage and five by marriage," and in another narration: "and seven by marriage," meaning His saying the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers, your daughters, your sisters, your paternal aunts, your maternal aunts, the daughters of your brother, and the daughters of your sister﴾ [An-Nisa: 23]. This is lineage. Then he means by marriage His saying, blessed and exalted: ﴿And your mothers who have nursed you, and your sisters through nursing, and the mothers of your wives, and your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship, [born] of your wives with whom you have consummated marriage — but if you have not consummated marriage with them, there is no blame upon you — and the wives of your sons who are from your loins, and that you combine two sisters, except what has already occurred﴾ [An-Nisa: 23], then He mentioned the married women. This may indicate that Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) meant: (p-448) "Forbidden by marriage is what is mentioned alongside it," so by "what is mentioned" he intended its principal part, which is marriage; not that nursing is marriage. Rather, nursing is the counterpart of lineage, and what is forbidden by lineage is forbidden by nursing according to the transmitted hadith on this. And whoever narrates "and five are forbidden by marriage" has dropped from the two verses the combining of two sisters and the married women, who are those with husbands.

Al-Zahrawi related an opinion: that lineage is through the sons, and marriage through the daughters.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This is good, and it is within the scope of what I have already mentioned. Ibn Sirin said: this verse was revealed concerning the Prophet ﷺ and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him), because lineage and marriage were combined between them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

Their combining of both is a bond of sanctity until the Day of Resurrection.

His saying: ﴿And your Lord is ever Powerful﴾ — the "kana" here is the one that indicates continuity both before and after, not one that gives only the past tense.

Then the Exalted mentioned their error in worshipping idols that possess for them neither harm nor benefit. His saying: ﴿And the disbeliever is ever a helper against his Lord﴾ has two interpretations: one of them is that *al-zahir* means the helper, so the verse means a rebuke of them for this, in that the disbelievers help others among the disbelievers against their Lord, and help Satan by obeying him and supporting him. This is the interpretation of Mujahid, al-Hasan, and Ibn Zayd. The second, which al-Tabari mentioned, is that *al-zahir* is a *fa'il* form from your saying "zahartu al-shay'" when you cast it behind your back and take it as something cast aside; so the meaning of the verse on this interpretation is the contempt for the disbelievers. "The disbeliever" in this verse is a generic noun. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) said: rather, it refers to a specific person, meaning Abu Jahl ibn Hisham.

(p-449) The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

It seems that Abu Jahl was the occasion of revelation, but the wording is general for the whole category.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿And We have not sent you﴾ to the end of the verse is a consolation to Muhammad ﷺ, meaning: do not concern yourself with them, and do not let your soul go in sighs out of eagerness for them; you are only a messenger who gives glad tidings to the believers of Paradise and warns the disbelievers of the Fire, and you are not held responsible for their faith, all of them.

Then He, the Exalted, commanded him to argue against them, removing the aspects of accusation, with His saying: ﴿I do not ask you for it any payment﴾, meaning: I do not seek wealth or any benefit that is specific to me. His saying the Exalted: ﴿except whoever wills﴾ — the apparent meaning here is that it is a disjunctive exception, and the meaning is: what I ask of you and seek from you is that whoever wills to be guided, believe, and take to the mercy of his Lord a path of salvation, let him do so. Al-Tabari said: the meaning is: I do not ask you for any reward except spending wealth in the way of Allah; this is what is asked, and it is the path to the Lord.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

The exception, on this reading, is like a connected one, as if he said: except the reward of whoever wills. The first interpretation is more apparent.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 25, verses 58–60:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And put your trust in the Living, who does not die, and glorify Him with His praise. And sufficient is He as Knower of the sins of His servants.﴾ ﴿He who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, then established Himself upon the Throne—the Most Merciful—so ask about Him one who is aware.﴾ ﴿And when it is said to them, "Prostrate yourselves to the Most Merciful," they say, "And what is the Most Merciful? Shall we prostrate to what you command us?" and it increases them in aversion.﴾

The meaning: Say to them, O Muhammad, this statement with which no doubt turns toward you, and do not be concerned by it. Give good tidings, warn, and put your trust in the Living, who does not die, for He is the one who takes charge of your support in all your affairs.

Then Exalted is He described Himself with the attribute that necessitates trust, in His saying: ﴿the Living who does not die﴾; for this meaning is specific to Allah, blessed and exalted, to the exclusion of everything in this world that bears the name "living." His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and glorify Him with His praise﴾ means: say, "Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him," that is, His transcendence is obligatory, and I say it with His praise.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever says 'Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him' one hundred times a day, his sins will be forgiven even if they were like the foam of the sea."
