Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 25, verses 61–63:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿Blessed is He who placed in the sky constellations and placed within it a lamp and a luminous moon.﴾ ﴿And it is He who made the night and the day alternating for whoever wishes to remember or wishes to be grateful.﴾ ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility, and when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace."﴾

When Quraysh made their question about God, may He be exalted, and about His name, which is al-Rahman, a question about something unknown, this verse was revealed, clearly stating His attributes by which He is known and which make it obligatory to acknowledge His divinity. The "burūj" (constellations) are those which the Arabs knew through experience, and every nation that dwells in the open country knows them. They are the months according to the philologists and those who calculate the times, and each constellation (burj) comprises two and a third lunar mansions (manāzil al-qamar), which God, blessed and exalted, mentioned in His saying: ﴿And for the moon We have determined stages﴾ [Yasin 36:39]. The Arabs call a high, self-sufficient building a "burj" by way of comparison with the constellations of the sky. From this is His saying, blessed and exalted: ﴿And even if you were in towers built high﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:78]. al-Akhtal said:

"As if it were a Roman tower, built by a builder with plaster, baked brick, and stones."

Some people said, regarding this verse in which we are: the "burūj" are the palaces in Paradise. al-A'mash said: the companions of 'Abd Allah used to recite it as "fī al-samā' qusūran" (in the sky, palaces). It was also said: the "burūj" are the great stars, which al-Tha'labi related from Abu Salih. This is similar to what we have explained, except that it is not condensed. But the claim that they are palaces in Paradise undermines the purpose of the verse, which is to draw attention to perceptible things by which proof is established against every denier of God or everyone ignorant of Him.

(p. 453) The majority of readers recited "sirājan" (a lamp), which is the sun. Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i, 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, 'Alqamah and al-A'mash recited "surujan" (lamps), which is the collective noun for all lights, and the moon was singled out for mention as an honour. al-Nakha'i, Ibn Wthab and al-A'mash also recited "surjan" with a sukūn on the rā'. Abu Ḥatim said: 'Iṣmah related from al-Ḥasan "wa-qumran" with a ḍammah on the qāf and a sukūn on the mīm. I do not know what he intended except that it be a plural like thamar and thumur. Abu 'Amr said: this is the reading of al-A'mash and al-Nakha'i.

His saying "khilfah" means: this succeeds that. In this sense is the saying of Zuhayr:

"Among them the gazelles and the wild cows walk in succession, and their young rise from every resting place."

And from this is the saying of another, describing a woman who moves from one dwelling in winter to another in summer, habitually:

"For her, at al-Matirun, when the ants have eaten what they gathered,
is an alternation, until, when she settles in the spring, she dwells in Jilliq, grape-vines,
in houses in the midst of a palace, around which olive trees have ripened."

(p. 454) Mujahid said: "khilfah" is from disagreement: this one is white and this one is black, similar to what we have mentioned. Mujahid and others said: ﴿for whoever wishes to remember﴾ means: to take warning from the created things and to thank God, blessed and exalted, for His blessings upon him in reason, thought and understanding. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, al-Ḥasan and Ibn 'Abbas said: its meaning is: for whoever wishes to remember what he missed of good, prayer and the like in one of them, so that he may make it up in the one that follows. Ḥamzah alone recited "yadhkura" with a sukūn on the dhāl and a ḍammah on the kāf; this is the reading of Ibn Wthab, Ṭalḥah and al-Nakha'i. The rest recited "yadhdhakkara" with a shaddah on the dhāl. In the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b it is "yatadhakkara" with an added tā'.

Then, when He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿for whoever wishes to remember or wishes to be grateful﴾, He went on to describe His servants, who are the people of remembrance and gratitude. "al-'Ibād" and "al-'Abīd" have the same meaning, except that "al-'Ibād" is used in contexts of honour. A group from 'Abd al-Qays were called "al-'Ibād" because Kisra made them kings apart from the Arabs. It was also said: because they worshipped along with the Christians of al-Ḥīrah, and so they became "the servants of God." 'Adi ibn Zayd al-'Ibadi is ascribed to them. al-Ḥasan recited "wa-'Ubud al-Rahman," as al-Tha'labi mentioned.

His saying, blessed and exalted: ﴿who walk﴾ is the predicate of an inchoative, and the meaning is: His servants, the true servants, are those who walk. His saying: ﴿walk upon the earth in humility﴾ is an expression for their life, the duration of their lives, and their conduct, and so it mentions the most important part of it, especially since moving about the earth involves associating with people and mixing with them. Then He said: "hawnan" (in humility), meaning that their whole affair is hawn, that is, gentle and good. Mujahid said: with forbearance and dignity. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: with obedience, chastity and humility. al-Ḥasan said: with forbearance, so that if the ignorant act ignorantly toward them, they do not act ignorantly in return. A group went to the view that "hawnan" is linked to His saying: ﴿walk upon the earth﴾, that is, walking itself is the hawn. It may be interpreted this way: that the character of the one who walks is gentle and suited to his walking, so the saying returns to what we have explained. As for the view that the intended meaning is the attribute of walking alone, it is false, because many a person walks gently and slowly while being a bald wolf. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) "used to walk with a forward lean, as if he were walking downhill" (and he, peace and blessings be upon him, was the most upright of men in this verse). His saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "Whoever among you walks in greed, let him walk slowly" — he intended this in regard to the state of his heart, not walking alone. Do you not see that the falsifiers who adorned themselves with religion clung only to the outward form of walking, until the poet said of them in censure:

"All of them walk slowly, all of them seek prey."

al-Zuhri said: haste in walking takes away the radiance of the face.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

He means swift, hurried haste, because it undermines dignity, and the good lies in moderation. Zayd ibn Aslam said: I used to ask about the interpretation of His saying, blessed and exalted: ﴿who walk upon the earth in humility﴾, but I found no cure in it, until I saw in a dream someone who came to me and said: "They are those who do not wish to cause corruption on the earth."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is an interpretation in terms of character. "Hawnan" means gentleness and moderation, and from it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Love your beloved with moderation (hawnan ma)..." the hadith. And His saying: ﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace."﴾ They differed about the interpretation of this. One group said: the addresser should say to the ignorant one "salaman" (peace) with this wording, that is, "We greet you with a greeting," or something similar, so that the governing element is a verb from the same root, according to the method of the grammarians. What I say is that His saying "qālū" (they say) is the governing element of "salaman," because the meaning is: they say this utterance. Mujahid said: the meaning of "salaman" is: a upright word, that is, he says to the ignorant person a word by which he repels him gently and softly. Those who held this interpretation said: the governing element of His saying "salaman" according to the method of the grammarians is that it has the sense of "qawlan" (a word). This verse was before the verse of the sword, so what concerns the unbelievers was abrogated from it (naskh, the cancellation of one ruling by a later revelation), and its courtesy remained for Muslims until the Day of Resurrection. Sibawayh mentioned abrogation in regard to this verse in his book, and he mentioned no other abrogation, and he preferred from it that the intended meaning is safety (salāmah), not greeting (taslīm), because the believers were never commanded to greet non-Muslims. The verse is Meccan, and the verse of the sword abrogated it.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

I saw in some of the books of histories that Ibrahim ibn al-Mahdi, who was among those inclined toward 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, said one day in the presence of al-Ma'mun, with a group present: "I used to see 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, in a dream, and I would say to him, 'Who are you?' He would say, 'I am 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.' I would go with him to a bridge, and he would go ahead of me to cross it, and I would say to him, 'You claim this matter through a woman, and we have more right to it than you.' I did not see in his reply any eloquence, as is related of him." Al-Ma'mun said: "And how did he answer you?" He said: "He would say to me, 'Salaman, salaman.'" The narrator said: It was as if Ibrahim ibn al-Mahdi did not remember the verse, or it had slipped from him at that time. So al-Ma'mun drew attention to the verse before those present, and said: "By God, O uncle, it is 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, and he answered you with the most eloquent reply." Ibrahim was saddened and ashamed, and his dream was undoubtedly true.

His saying: ﴿walk upon the earth in humility﴾ is an expression for their life, the duration of their lives, and their conduct, and so it mentions the most important part of it, especially since moving about the earth involves associating with people and mixing with them. Then He said: "hawnan" (in humility), meaning that their whole affair is hawn, that is, gentle and good. Mujahid said: with forbearance and dignity. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: with obedience, chastity and humility. al-Ḥasan said: with forbearance, so that if the ignorant act ignorantly toward them, they do not act ignorantly in return. A group went to the view that "hawnan" is linked to His saying: ﴿walk upon the earth﴾, that is, walking itself is the hawn. It may be interpreted this way: that the character of the one who walks is gentle and suited to his walking, so the saying returns to what we have explained. As for the view that the intended meaning is the attribute of walking alone, it is false, because many a person walks gently and slowly while being a bald wolf. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) "used to walk with a forward lean, as if he were walking downhill" (and he, peace and blessings be upon him, was the most upright of men in this verse). His saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "Whoever among you walks in greed, let him walk slowly" — he intended this in regard to the state of his heart, not walking alone. Do you not see that the falsifiers who adorned themselves with religion clung only to the outward form of walking, until the poet said of them in censure:

"All of them walk slowly, all of them seek prey."

al-Zuhri said: haste in walking takes away the radiance of the face.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

He means swift, hurried haste, because it undermines dignity, and the good lies in moderation. Zayd ibn Aslam said: I used to ask about the interpretation of His saying, blessed and exalted: ﴿who walk upon the earth in humility﴾, but I found no cure in it, until I saw in a dream someone who came to me and said: "They are those who do not wish to cause corruption on the earth."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is an interpretation in terms of character. "Hawnan" means gentleness and moderation, and from it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Love your beloved with moderation (hawnan ma)..." the hadith. And His saying: ﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace."﴾ They differed about the interpretation of this. One group said: the addresser should say to the ignorant one "salaman" (peace) with this wording, that is, "We greet you with a greeting," or something similar, so that the governing element is a verb from the same root, according to the method of the grammarians. What I say is that His saying "qālū" (they say) is the governing element of "salaman," because the meaning is: they say this utterance. Mujahid said: the meaning of "salaman" is: a upright word, that is, he says to the ignorant person a word by which he repels him gently and softly. Those who held this interpretation said: the governing element of His saying "salaman" according to the method of the grammarians is that it has the sense of "qawlan" (a word). This verse was before the verse of the sword, so what concerns the unbelievers was abrogated from it (naskh, the cancellation of one ruling by a later revelation), and its courtesy remained for Muslims until the Day of Resurrection. Sibawayh mentioned abrogation in regard to this verse in his book, and he mentioned no other abrogation, and he preferred from it that the intended meaning is safety (salāmah), not greeting (taslīm), because the believers were never commanded to greet non-Muslims. The verse is Meccan, and the verse of the sword abrogated it.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

I saw in some of the books of histories that Ibrahim ibn al-Mahdi, who was among those inclined toward 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, said one day in the presence of al-Ma'mun, with a group present: "I used to see 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, in a dream, and I would say to him, 'Who are you?' He would say, 'I am 'Ali ibn Abi Talib.' I would go with him to a bridge, and he would go ahead of me to cross it, and I would say to him, 'You claim this matter through a woman, and we have more right to it than you.' I did not see in his reply any eloquence, as is related of him." Al-Ma'mun said: "And how did he answer you?" He said: "He would say to me, 'Salaman, salaman.'" The narrator said: It was as if Ibrahim ibn al-Mahdi did not remember the verse, or it had slipped from him at that time. So al-Ma'mun drew attention to the verse before those present, and said: "By God, O uncle, it is 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, and he answered you with the most eloquent reply." Ibrahim was saddened and ashamed, and his dream was undoubtedly true.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 25, verses 61–63:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿Blessed is He who placed in the sky constellations and placed within it a lamp and a luminous moon.﴾ ﴿And it is He who made the night and the day alternating for whoever wishes to remember or wishes to be grateful.﴾ ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility, and when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace."﴾

When Quraysh made their question about God, may He be exalted, and about His name, which is al-Rahman, a question about something unknown, this verse was revealed, clearly stating His attributes by which He is known and which make it obligatory to acknowledge His divinity. The "burūj" (constellations) are those which the Arabs knew through experience, and every nation that dwells in the open country knows them. They are the months according to the philologists and those who calculate the times, and each constellation (burj) comprises two and a third lunar mansions (manāzil al-qamar), which God, blessed and exalted, mentioned in His saying: ﴿And for the moon We have determined stages﴾ [Yasin 36:39]. The Arabs call a high, self-sufficient building a "burj" by way of comparison with the constellations of the sky. From this is His saying, blessed and exalted: ﴿And even if you were in towers built high﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:78]. al-Akhtal said:

"As if it were a Roman tower, built by a builder with plaster, baked brick, and stones."

Some people said, regarding this verse in which we are: the "burūj" are the palaces in Paradise. al-A'mash said: the companions of 'Abd Allah used to recite it as "fī al-samā' qusūran" (in the sky, palaces). It was also said: the "burūj" are the great stars, which al-Tha'labi related from Abu Salih. This is similar to what we have explained, except that it is not condensed. But the claim that they are palaces in Paradise undermines the purpose of the verse, which is to draw attention to perceptible things by which proof is established against every denier of God or everyone ignorant of Him.

(p. 453) The majority of readers recited "sirājan" (a lamp), which is the sun. Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i, 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, 'Alqamah and al-A'mash recited "surujan" (lamps), which is the collective noun for all lights, and the moon was singled out for mention as an honour. al-Nakha'i, Ibn Wthab and al-A'mash also recited "surjan" with a sukūn on the rā'. Abu Ḥatim said: 'Iṣmah related from al-Ḥasan "wa-qumran" with a ḍammah on the qāf and a sukūn on the mīm. I do not know what he intended except that it be a plural like thamar and thumur. Abu 'Amr said: this is the reading of al-A'mash and al-Nakha'i.

His saying "khilfah" means: this succeeds that. In this sense is the saying of Zuhayr:

"Among them the gazelles and the wild cows walk in succession, and their young rise from every resting place."

And from this is the saying of another, describing a woman who moves from one dwelling in winter to another in summer, habitually:

"For her, at al-Matirun, when the ants have eaten what they gathered,
is an alternation, until, when she settles in the spring, she dwells in Jilliq, grape-vines,
in houses in the midst of a palace, around which olive trees have ripened."

(p. 454) Mujahid said: "khilfah" is from disagreement: this one is white and this one is black, similar to what we have mentioned. Mujahid and others said: ﴿for whoever wishes to remember﴾ means: to take warning from the created things and to thank God, blessed and exalted, for His blessings upon him in reason, thought and understanding. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, al-Ḥasan and Ibn 'Abbas said: its meaning is: for whoever wishes to remember what he missed of good, prayer and the like in one of them, so that he may make it up in the one that follows. Ḥamzah alone recited "yadhkura" with a sukūn on the dhāl and a ḍammah on the kāf; this is the reading of Ibn Wthab, Ṭalḥah and al-Nakha'i. The rest recited "yadhdhakkara" with a shaddah on the dhāl. In the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b it is "yatadhakkara" with an added tā'.

Then, when He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿for whoever wishes to remember or wishes to be grateful﴾, He went on to describe His servants, who are the people of remembrance and gratitude. "al-'Ibād" and "al-'Abīd" have the same meaning, except that "al-'Ibād" is used in contexts of honour. A group from 'Abd al-Qays were called "al-'Ibād" because Kisra made them kings apart from the Arabs. It was also said: because they worshipped along with the Christians of al-Ḥīrah, and so they became "the servants of God." 'Adi ibn Zayd al-'Ibadi is ascribed to them. al-Ḥasan recited "wa-'Ubud al-Rahman," as al-Tha'labi mentioned.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 25, verses 64–66:

His the Exalted's saying:

﴿And those who spend the night before their Lord, prostrating and standing [in worship]﴾ ﴿And those who say, "Our Lord, avert from us the punishment of Hell; indeed, its punishment is ever a lasting torment"﴾ ﴿Indeed, it is evil as a place of settlement and residence﴾

This is a verse that contains encouragement to stand in prayer during the night (qiyam al-layl). Al-Hasan said: "When He finished describing their days, He described their nights in this verse." Some people said: "Whoever prays the late night prayer (al-'isha' al-akhira), then performs the even units (shaf') and the witr, is included in this verse."

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

"However, this inclusion is not complete." Abu al-Barahsam read: "sujudan" (prostrations).

The Exalted praised them for their supplication to avert the punishment of Hell, and this is evidence of the soundness of their creed and faith, and of their deeds being in accordance with it. "Gharaman" means: constant, heavy, ruinous. From it comes "gharam al-hubb" (the torment of love). From it is the saying of al-A'sha:

"If He punishes, the punishment will be gharaman; and if He gives abundantly, He does not care."

And the saying of Bishr ibn Abi Khazim:

"And the day of al-Nisar and the day of al-Jifar, they were a punishment and were gharaman."

Most of the people read "muqaman" with a damma on the mim, from iqama (dwelling), and from it is the saying of the poet:

"Greet the muqam, and greet the dweller of the abode."

A group read "maqaman" with a fatha on the mim, from qama yaqumu (to stand), so Hell is the place of standing for them. The first reading is more eloquent and better known.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 25, verses 67–70:

His Mighty and Majestic words:

﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor niggardly, but keep to a balance between that﴾ ﴿And those who do not call upon another god besides Allah, nor kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right, nor commit adultery; and whoever does that will meet a penalty﴾ ﴿The punishment will be doubled for him on the Day of Resurrection, and he will abide therein in humiliation﴾ ﴿Except for one who repents, believes, and does righteous work; for those, Allah will change their evil deeds into good deeds, and Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾

The exegetes have differed concerning this verse about spending. The statement of most of them is that the one who is not extravagant (lā yusrif) is the one who spends in obedience even if he goes to excess, and the extravagant (musrif) is the one who spends in disobedience even if his spending is little; and that the niggardly (muqtir) is the one who withholds a right that is due upon him. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and Ibn Zayd. 'Awn ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Utba said: extravagance (al-isrāf) is to spend the wealth of another than yourself. Other sayings besides these are not connected to the wording of the verse. Mixing obedience and disobedience with extravagance and niggardliness in this matter is open to question; the correct view is to say: spending on disobedience is a matter the Sharia has prohibited, whether little or much, and likewise transgressing upon the property of others. These described people are far removed from that. The discipline in this verse concerns spending on acts of obedience in permissible matters. The Sharia's discipline in this is that a person should not go to excess to the point of neglecting another right or dependents and the like, and also that he should not restrict and be niggardly to the point of starving his dependents and being excessively miserly. The good in this is the balance (qawām), that is, moderation (al-ʿadl), and the balance differs for each person according to his dependents and his condition, his lightness of burden, his patience and his endurance in earning, or the opposite of these qualities. The best of matters is the middle of them. For this reason, "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) allowed Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) to give charity with all his wealth," because that was a middle course relative to his endurance and patience in religion; and he forbade others from doing so. Excellently did Ibrahim al-Nakha'i say: "It is the one who does not starve (his dependents) nor leaves them naked, and does not spend an expenditure that people say: he has been extravagant." Yazid ibn Abi Habib said: "They are those who do not wear clothes for beauty, nor eat food for pleasure." 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan said to 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz (may Allah be pleased with him) when he married him to his daughter Fatima: "What is your expenditure?" 'Umar said to him: "A good deed between two bad ones," then he recited this verse. Yazid ibn Habib also said regarding this verse: "Those are the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ); they did not eat food for luxury and pleasure, nor wear garments for beauty, but they wanted from food what would satisfy their hunger and strengthen them for worshipping their Lord, and from clothing what would cover their nakedness and shield them from heat and cold." 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "It is enough extravagance for a person that he should buy and eat whatever he desires." In the Sunan of Ibn Majah, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, among extravagance is that you eat whatever you desire." And the poet said:

Do not exaggerate in any matter, but moderate; Both extremes of the affairs are blameworthy.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Abu Bakr, Mujahid, and Hafs from 'Asim read "yaqturū" with a fatha on the ya and a kasra on the ta. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read with a fatha on the ya and a damma on the ta, which is the reading of al-Hasan and al-A'mash, and 'Asim with a variant. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman read with a damma on the ya and a fatha on the ta.

Abu 'Amr and the people read "qawāman" with a fatha on the qaf, meaning moderate (muʿtadil). Hassan ibn 'Abd al-Rahman read it with a kasra on the qaf, meaning sufficient, a firm measure and the foundation of a condition. "Qawāman" is the predicate of "kāna," and its subject is implied, meaning: the spending. Al-Farra' permitted that its subject be His saying "bayna dhālika" (between that).

His Most High saying: ﴿And those who do not call upon another god besides Allah﴾ to the end of the verse, is a removal of His believing servants from the attributes of the disbelievers in: their worship of idols, their killing of souls by burying daughters alive, and other injustices, assassinations and raids, and by fornication, which was permitted among them. Regarding verses like this, 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "I said one day to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): Which sin is greatest? He said: That you set up a rival to Allah while He created you. I said: Then what? He said: That you kill your child lest it eat with you. I said: Then what? He said: That you commit adultery with your neighbour's wife." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

By killing and fornication, those sinners among the believers enter into this verse, and for them is a threat in proportion to that. The right by which a soul is killed is the killing of a soul, apostasy after faith, and adultery after being married (ihsān); and the disbelief which is not preceded by faith is that of the combatants.

"Al-athām" in the speech of the Arabs means punishment, and Ibn Zayd interpreted this verse with it, and from it is the poet's saying:

May Allah repay Ibn 'Urwa, since he has become one who disobeys parents, and disobedience has its penalty.

That is: recompense and punishment. 'Ikrima, 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, and Mujahid said: "Athām" is a valley in Hell, this is its name, and Allah the Most High has made it a punishment for the disbelievers.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read "yuḍāʿaf" and "yakhlud" with jazm. Ibn Kathir, Abu Ja'far, al-Hasan, and Ibn 'Amir read "yuḍaʿʿaf" with a shadda on the ʿayn and omission of the alif, and with jazm on "yuḍaʿʿaf" and "wa-yakhlud." Talha ibn Sulayman read "nuḍaʿʿif" with a damma on the nun and a kasra on the shaddated ʿayn, "al-ʿadhāb" in the accusative, and "wa-yakhlud" with jazm, which is the reading of Abu Ja'far. Talha ibn Sulayman also read "wa-takhlud" with a ta, in the sense of addressing the disbeliever with that. It is narrated from Abu 'Amr: "wa-yukhlad" with a damma on the initial ya and a fatha on the lam, but Abu 'Ali said: this is an error on the side of transmission. "Yuḍāʿaf" with jazm is a substitute for "yalqa," and Sibawayh said: the doubling of the punishment is the meeting with the penalty. The poet said:

When you come to us, you will visit us in our homes, and you will find firewood, thick, and a fire blazing.

His Most High saying: ﴿Except for one who repents﴾ to the end of the verse. There is no disagreement among the scholars that the exception applies to the disbeliever and the adulterer. They differed regarding a Muslim killer. The majority of scholars said: he has repentance. This group took as their foundation His saying: ﴿And He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [An-Nisa: 48], so the killer falls under the Will like the other repentant sinners. They interpret the "abiding" (khulūd) mentioned in the verse on killing in Surat an-Nisa as meaning lasting for a period, like the lasting of dynasties and the like. Abu Hurayra narrated for the one who kills a hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ). It was said: this verse was revealed concerning Wahshi, the killer of Hamza (may Allah be pleased with him), and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said so. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) and others said: there is no repentance for the killer. The statement of most of them is that the one who is not extravagant (lā yusrif) is the one who spends in obedience even if he goes to excess, and the extravagant (musrif) is the one who spends in disobedience even if his spending is little; and that the niggardly (muqtir) is the one who withholds a right that is due upon him. These described people are far removed from that. The discipline in this verse concerns spending on acts of obedience in permissible matters. The Sharia's discipline in this is that a person should not go to excess to the point of neglecting another right or dependents and the like, and also that he should not restrict and be niggardly to the point of starving his dependents and being excessively miserly. The good in this is the balance (qawām), that is, moderation (al-ʿadl), and the balance differs for each person according to his dependents and his condition, his lightness of burden, his patience and his endurance in earning, or the opposite of these qualities. The best of matters is the middle of them. Yazid ibn Abi Habib said: "They are those who do not wear clothes for beauty, nor eat food for pleasure." 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan said to 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz (may Allah be pleased with him) when he married him to his daughter Fatima: "What is your expenditure?" 'Umar said to him: "A good deed between two bad ones," then he recited this verse. In the Sunan of Ibn Majah, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, among extravagance is that you eat whatever you desire." And the poet said:

Do not exaggerate in any matter, but moderate; Both extremes of the affairs are blameworthy.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read with a fatha on the ya and a damma on the ta, which is the reading of al-Hasan and al-A'mash, and 'Asim with a variant. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman read with a damma on the ya and a fatha on the ta.

Talha ibn Sulayman read "nuḍaʿʿif" with a damma on the nun and a kasra on the shaddated ʿayn, "al-ʿadhāb" in the accusative, and "wa-yakhlud" with jazm, which is the reading of Abu Ja'far. Talha ibn Sulayman also read "wa-takhlud" with a ta, in the sense of addressing the disbeliever with that. It is narrated from Abu 'Amr: "wa-yukhlad" with a damma on the initial ya and a fatha on the lam, but Abu 'Ali said: this is an error on the side of transmission. "Yuḍāʿaf" with jazm is a substitute for "yalqa," and Sibawayh said: the doubling of the punishment is the meeting with the penalty. The poet said:

When you come to us, you will visit us in our homes, and you will find firewood, thick, and a fire blazing.

His Most High saying: ﴿Except for one who repents﴾ to the end of the verse. There is no disagreement among the scholars that the exception applies to the disbeliever and the adulterer. They differed regarding a Muslim killer. The majority of scholars said: he has repentance. This group took as their foundation His saying: ﴿And He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [An-Nisa: 48], so the killer falls under the Will like the other repentant sinners. They interpret the "abiding" (khulūd) mentioned in the verse on killing in Surat an-Nisa as meaning lasting for a period, like the lasting of dynasties and the like. Abu Hurayra narrated for the one who kills a hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ). It was said: this verse was revealed concerning Wahshi, the killer of Hamza (may Allah be pleased with him), and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said so. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) and others said: there is no repentance for the killer. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "The repentance mentioned in this verse is intended for the polytheists, because when it was revealed, groups of the polytheists said: How can we enter Islam when we have done all of this? So ﴿except for one who repents﴾ was revealed, and ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah﴾ [Az-Zumar: 53] was revealed, and I never saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rejoice at anything as he rejoiced at these and at Surat al-Fath." Others besides Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) who said there is no repentance for the killer said: this verse is abrogated by the verse in Surat an-Nisa; this was said by Zayd ibn Thabit, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr also narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both). Abu al-Jawza' said: "I accompanied Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) for thirteen years, and I did not see anything of the Qur'an except that I asked him about it, and I never heard him say: Allah the Blessed and Most High says of a sin: I will not forgive it."

His Most High saying: ﴿Allah will change their evil deeds into good deeds﴾. Its meaning: He makes their deeds, in place of their earlier disobediences, obedience, so that this becomes a cause of Allah's mercy toward them, the Mighty and Majestic. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Ibn Zayd, and al-Hasan, and they refuted those who said: it refers to the Day of Resurrection, for whoever among the monotheists desires His forgiveness, He changes the evil deeds into good deeds. This is the interpretation of Ibn al-Musayyab of this verse.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

And this is the meaning of the generosity of pardon.

Ibn Abi 'Abla read "yubdilu" with a sukun on the ba and lightening of the dal.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 25, verses 71–74:**

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And whoever repents and does righteous deeds, then indeed he turns back to Allah with a [sincere] return.﴾ ﴿And those who do not bear witness to falsehood, and when they pass by idle talk (laghw), they pass by with dignity.﴾ ﴿And those who, when they are reminded of the signs of their Lord, do not fall upon them deaf and blind.﴾ ﴿And those who say, "Our Lord, grant us from among our spouses and our offspring the coolness of the eyes, and make us a leader (imam) for the God-fearing."﴾

This wording emphasizes the matter of repentance. The meaning is: whoever repents has indeed grasped a firm matter. This is like when you say to someone whose words are praised regarding a matter, "You have certainly said a saying, O so-and-so." Likewise, the meaning of the verse is praise of repentance, as if He said: "Indeed, he finds a great door of relief and forgiveness." Then the verses continue describing the servants of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, who are believers, by negating for them the bearing of witness to falsehood (zur).

In this verse, "yashhadun" (they witness) in its apparent meaning is: they are present at and attend [such gatherings]. "Zur" is every falsehood that has been embellished and adorned. Its greatest form is shirk (associating partners with Allah), and this is how al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd explained it. It also includes singing, and this is how Mujahid explained it. It also includes lying, and this is how Ibn Jurayj explained it. Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, and Muhammad ibn Ali said: the meaning is "they do not bear witness to falsehood," so it is from testimony (shahada), not from attending (mushahada), and "zur" is lying.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The one who bears false witness, whether he is present at it or gives it, is a sinner (fajara). The first meaning is more general, but the second meaning is more immersed in sins and more severe.

"Laghw" is every worthless thing of action or speech. It includes singing, amusement and other things close to them. It includes the foolishness of the polytheists and their harm to the believers, the mention of women, and other kinds of wrongdoing (munkar). "Kiraman" means: turning away, showing disdain, disregarding these things, and bearing patiently the harm that comes from them. It is narrated that "Abdullah ibn Mas'ud heard singing, so he quickened his pace and left. This reached the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: 'Indeed, the son of Umm Abd has become noble (karim),' and he recited the verse."

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

As for the Muslim who passes by a wrongdoing, his nobility is to change it, and the limits of changing it are well known.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And those who, when they are reminded of the signs of their Lord﴾ means: they are reminded through the Qur'an of their afterlife and their return. His saying ﴿do not fall upon them deaf and blind﴾ admits of two interpretations. One of them: the meaning is that their going out [to it] is not in this manner; rather, their going out is in prostration and weeping. This is like when you say, "Zayd did not go out to the battle in fear," meaning: he went out bold and forward. Or it is as if the one who falls deaf and blind is the hypocrite or the doubter. The second interpretation, to which al-Tabari went, is that ﴿fall upon them deaf and blind﴾ is a description of the disbelievers. It is an expression of their turning away and their effort in that, and it is paired with your saying, "So-and-so sat reviling me," and "So-and-so stood weeping," while you did not intend to report sitting or standing, but these are preparatory phrases in speech and expression.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is as if the listener to the reminder is upright in posture and straight in affair. When he turns away and goes astray, that is "kharur" (falling), which is falling without order or arrangement. Although the one who falls prostrate has been likened to it, its origin is that it is without order.

Then He praised the believers in the situation of supplication to Him, that they ask that the eyes be cooled by family and offspring. "Qurrat al-ayn" (coolness of the eyes) may be from "qarar" (settling), and it may be from "qarr" (coldness), and the latter is more well known, because the tears of joy are cold and the tears of grief are hot. From this it is said: "May Allah cool your eye (aqarra Allahu aynaka)," and "May Allah heat the eye of the enemy (askhana Allahu ayn al-'aduww)." The coolness of the eyes in spouses and offspring is that a person sees them obeying Allah, Blessed and Exalted. This was said by Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, and Hadrami. Al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad explained the aspect of this by saying that at the beginning of Islam, a son would become Muslim while his father was a disbeliever, or a husband while his wife was a disbeliever, so the coolness of their eyes lay in the faith of their beloved ones.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn Amir and al-Hasan read "wa-dhurriyyatina" (with the plural), while Abu Amr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Talha and Isa read "wa-dhurriyyatina" (with the singular).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and make us a leader (imam) for the God-fearing﴾ It was said: it is the plural of "amm," like "qa'im" and "qiyam." It was also said: it is the singular of a collective noun, meaning: make the God-fearing follow us. This is not possible unless the one who supplicates is himself God-fearing and an example. This is the intention of the supplicant. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: they did not seek leadership, but rather that they be examples in religion. This is good to seek and strive for.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 25, verses 75–77:

His the Mighty and Majestic's saying:

﴿Those will be rewarded with the lofty chamber for what they endured, and they will be met therein with greetings and peace.﴾ ﴿Abiding therein; how excellent a place of settlement and dwelling.﴾ ﴿Say: "My Lord would not care for you were it not for your supplication. But you have denied, so the punishment will inevitably come."﴾

Ubayy ibn Ka'b recited "yujāzawna" (yujazawna) with an alif, and "al-ghurfa" (the chamber) is among the dwellings of Paradise. It is the chambers above chambers, and it is a noun of genus (ism jins), as the poet said:

"Were it not for the dark-hued (al-ḥabba al-samrā') I would not have dismounted in your valley."

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and Abu 'Amr recited "wayulaqqawna" with a damma on the yā' (ya), a fatḥa on the lām, and a shadda on the qāf. This is the reading of Abu Ja'far, Shayba, and al-Hasan. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Talha, and Muhammad al-Yamani recited it "wayalqawna" with a fatḥa on the yā', a sukūn on the lām, and a lightened qāf, and this was narrated from the Prophet ﷺ. There is a difference of narration from 'Asim.

As for His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Say: "My Lord would not care for you..."﴾, the verse is a command to Muhammad ﷺ to address them with it. The word "mā" can carry the sense of negation and can carry the sense of affirmation (taqrīr), and the statement in itself admits several interpretations:

The first is that the verse, up to His saying ﴿were it not for your supplication﴾, is an address to all people, as if He said to the Quraysh among them: "Allah does not heed you, nor does He look upon you, were it not for your worship of Him, if indeed it existed. And blessings and peace be upon our master Muhammad, and upon his family and all his companions.
